faq.q: What is the first step in a conscious adult who is choking?

faq.a: It shows whether ventilation is occurring; low end‑tidal CO₂ indicates airway obstruction or inadequate breathing.
faq.q: Why is capnography useful in asphyxiation?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents after choking on a mango seed; what is your immediate action? — Perform Heimlich manoeuvre; if unsuccessful, prepare for laryngoscopy or surgical airway.

A child is found unresponsive after a house fire; SpO₂ is 85 % on room air. What does this indicate and how do you manage? — Severe hypoxaemia from smoke inhalation; give high‑flow O₂, consider intubation, assess for airway burns.

During CPR on a drowning victim, you notice a faint breath sound on the left. What does this suggest and what is your next step? — Possible airway obstruction or pneumothorax; check for obstruction, consider needle decompression if tension pneumothorax suspected.

An unconscious patient has a rigid neck and no breath sounds bilaterally. What is the most likely cause and immediate management? — Possible cervical spine injury with airway compromise; perform jaw‑thrust, insert nasopharyngeal airway, protect spine, call for surgical airway.

Why is epinephrine avoided in a patient with isolated choking but no cardiac arrest? — Epinephrine raises heart rate and blood pressure but does not relieve airway obstruction; focus on mechanical clearance first.

A patient with severe asthma presents with wheeze and cyanosis. How do you differentiate this from asphyxiation? — Asthma shows expiratory wheeze and responds to bronchodilators; asphyxiation often has absent breath sounds and no wheeze.

In a low‑resource clinic, you lack a laryngoscope. How can you secure the airway in a choking adult? — Continue repeated Heimlich manoeuvres; if unsuccessful, perform cricothyrotomy using a scalpel and bougie if available.
What laboratory finding may be misleading in carbon monoxide poisoning presenting as asphyxiation? — Normal PaO₂; CO binds hemoglobin, so arterial oxygen content is low despite normal PaO₂.
ai.title: Asphyxiation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Asphyxiation is failure of oxygen delivery to tissues, leading to hypoxia and possible death. Recognise causes, rapid assessment, and emergency management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Immediate loss of consciousness within seconds to minutes
Cardiac arrest follows if not reversed
Brain injury can become irreversible after 4–6 minutes of no flow
sections.p: Asphyxiation occurs when the airway or respiratory function is blocked, preventing adequate oxygen uptake. It can be sudden (e.g., choking) or progressive (e.g., severe asthma). In low‑resource settings, common causes include choking on food, strangulation, drowning, and inhalation of smoke or toxic gases.

b: Airway obstruction → no ventilation → hypoxaemia → cellular death
Hypoxaemia leads to metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, and myocardial depression
Rapid reversal of obstruction restores perfusion and prevents permanent injury
sections.p: The pathophysiology is a mismatch between oxygen demand and supply. The body first compensates with tachypnea, then cyanosis, then loss of consciousness. Recognise the three clinical stages: early (tachypnea, agitation), middle (cyanosis, bradycardia), late (agonal breathing, cardiac arrest).

b: History: time of event, witnessed loss of consciousness, type of exposure, known allergies or anatomical abnormalities
Examination: look for stridor, drooling, inability to speak, cyanosis, unequal chest movement
Immediate priority: restore airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs)
sections.p: In the ward, patients may present after a choking episode, near‑drowning, or exposure to smoke. In low‑resource hospitals, advanced airway equipment may be lacking, so basic maneuvers are critical.

b: Heimlich manoeuvre is first‑line for conscious adult choking
Back blows and chest thrusts for infants
If unconscious, open airway with jaw‑thrust, consider nasopharyngeal airway if no facial trauma
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to act quickly, differentiate causes, and know simple adjuncts when equipment is scarce.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (cyanosis, altered mental status) and bedside monitoring (pulse, respiratory rate).

t.b: Is the patient hypoxic? – SpO₂ < 90 % confirms inadequate oxygenation; guide need for supplemental O₂.
Is ventilation adequate? – End‑tidal CO₂ < 35 mmHg suggests hypoventilation or airway obstruction.
What is the severity of hypoxaemia and acidosis? – PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or pH < 7.35 indicates significant respiratory compromise.
Is there pneumothorax or pulmonary infiltrate? – Look for collapsed lung or aspiration changes.

b: Conscious choking: Heimlich manoeuvre (abdominal thrusts) – rapid expulsion of foreign body.
Infant choking: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts – repeat until object expelled or patient becomes unconscious.
Unconscious patient: open airway, suction if visible obstruction, consider nasopharyngeal airway.
Give high‑flow oxygen (face mask or nasal cannula) – aim SpO₂ > 94 %.
If cardiac arrest: start CPR immediately, 30 compressions : 2 breaths, consider advanced airway when available.
sections.p: Treat the cause first, then support oxygenation and circulation. In low‑resource settings, use simple, reproducible techniques.

t.b: Will it raise SpO₂? – Improves tissue oxygenation; if no response, suspect airway obstruction still present.

b: Asthma exacerbation – bronchospasm, treat with bronchodilators; airway is not obstructed.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, treat with anticoagulation; no foreign body.
Anaphylaxis – airway edema, treat with epinephrine; not a mechanical blockage.
sections.p: Conditions that cause similar respiratory distress but have different management.

b: Pulse oximetry can be falsely high in carbon monoxide poisoning; consider CO‑Hb measurement if suspicion.
Normal chest X‑ray does not rule out airway obstruction; always assess clinically.
sections.p: Certain signs may appear normal early, giving false reassurance.
